_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 5 Tidy Programs. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (tidy programs; reset first; change the number; test then test again; the Scratch names and the number inside a block), in the lesson's own examples: the five-block jump program, the cat left two squares along and big, the flower at square 3, and the repeat that repeats a spin. Where a program ends is the LESSON'S OWN arithmetic, not the film's: ART.run and ART.walkEnd are asked once, beside the constants, so the tidy version and the untidy one are shown ending in the same place by the kit.
title: Tidy Programs
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Understand the benefit of editing programs to make them clear and concise, including removing unused commands or combining duplicated commands.
Know how to develop programs that include code to reset objects to their original state (initialisation).
Know how to make a change within a block of code to achieve desired outcomes in programs, such as changing the number of steps a sprite moves.
Know how to test and debug programs so that they run and produce the desired output.

beats.say: Jump, jump, jump, wait, say hello. That program has five blocks, and one does nothing.

at.long: Jump, jump, jump, wait, say hello

beats.say: Repeat 3 times, jump, say hello. Three blocks, and the cat does exactly the same.
Here is a program with five blocks: jump, jump, jump, wait, say hello.

at.list: jump, jump, jump, wait, say hello

beats.say: The wait block does nothing here. It is an unused command, so take it out.
Jump, jump, jump is the same block three times. Combine them into repeat 3 times, jump.
Three blocks now. The cat jumps three times and says hello, exactly as before.

at.does: jumps three times and says hello

beats.say: Shorter does not mean it does less. It is easier to read and to change.
The last program left the cat two squares along, and bigger than it started.
Run move right, then jump. The moves are right, but the place is wrong.
Put a go home block at the top. The cat is back at the start, normal size.
Now move right, jump ends where it should, every single time.
Putting things back to their starting state is called initialisation.
Sometimes the blocks are right and only a number is wrong.
The flower is at square 3. Move right 1, jump, move right 1 stops at square 2.
Change the first number from 1 to 2. Change one number, and nothing else.

at.change: Change the first number from 1 to 2

beats.say: Run it again. Right 2, jump, right 1 stops at 3, right on the flower.
No block moved. Only the number inside one block changed.
Testing is running a program to see what it really does.
Debugging is finding what went wrong, and then fixing it.
This one says repeat 3 times, spin, say hello. We wanted three jumps.
The repeat repeats a spin. That block is the bug, so change spin to jump.
Now run it again. A fix you have not tested is a fix you do not know works.
Your blocks have other names too. Scratch is the program most schools use.
Move right is move 10 steps. Jump is change y by 50. Spin is turn 90 degrees.
Go home is go to x: 0 y: 0. Repeat 3 times is repeat 3. Same jobs, real names.
Some blocks hold a number you can change. Move holds steps. Wait holds seconds.
Set volume holds one too. Volume is how loud a sound is, from 0 to 100.
A tidy program has no unused block and no duplicate left written out.
Go home first: that is initialisation. Then change one number inside a block.
Test after every change you make. The run is the test.
